extracted.intended_audience: general educated public and public-health/hygiene professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing claims and evidence about the sanitary (hygienic) value of plants and plantations for air quality and public health, including laboratory/field measurements (CO2, O2, ozone), enclosed-space experiments (winter-garden), and broader psychological, soil, and microclimatic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbonic acid (CO2) as indoor air-quality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use carbonic acid (CO2) concentration as the criterion of the quality of the air in apartments; 'One per mille marks the boundary-line between good and bad air in a room.' Very bad air in inhabited rooms has been found to amount to from three to five per mille.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report measured ranges (open air ≈ 3–4 parts in 10,000; very bad indoor air 3–5 per mille). Use CO2 measurements to regulate ventilation. Cite historical measurements and compare with standards when judging whether air is 'bad'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-air atmospheric composition largely unaffected by vegetation (scale/mixing consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetation exercises no perceptible influence upon the composition of the atmosphere in the open air because atmospheric mixing and the mass of the air dilute any local production/consumption of gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret open-air CO2 and O2 data in light of atmospheric mobility (average velocities cited) and the huge mass of air; do not expect measurable differences between desert and oasis or between city and country except under exceptional meteorological conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological insignificance of small oxygen concentration changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Small changes (one or two percent) in atmospheric oxygen are of little physiological consequence to healthy people; the quantity of oxygen we inhale depends more on respiratory regulation than on slight variations in atmospheric oxygen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overinterpret small measured differences in O2 (e.g., 21% vs 22–23%) as having major health effects for healthy individuals. Cite experimental work (Lavoisier, Regnault, Reiset) showing animals did not consume more oxygen when placed in oxygen-rich air; note compensatory changes in respiration rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ozone not demonstrably hygienically valuable indoors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ozone cannot be detected in dwellings and there is no demonstrable connection between indoor ozone levels and the appearance or disappearance of diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims that indoor ozone explains disease patterns skeptically; reference ozone-station reports (Konigsberg) and experimental/observational negative results. Recognize ozone's atmospheric role as an oxidizer but not as an effective indoor disinfectant at ambient concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/biomass/time requirement: potted plants insufficient for air purification
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of a few potted plants to change indoor air composition is negligible: 'The power of twenty-pots of plants would not be nearly sufficient to neutralize the carbonic acid exhaled by a single child in a given time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plant-based remedies by comparing plant photosynthetic rates, total biomass, and timescales against human metabolic CO2 production. Use quantitative estimates to judge whether plantings are sufficient to affect air quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation is more effective than plants for indoor air improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot dispense with the greatest cleanliness and best ventilation in homes, nor can one essentially change room air by means of plants in pots and foliage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize ventilation and hygiene measures when addressing indoor air quality; view plants as supplementary/aesthetic rather than primary engineering solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/aesthetic effects of plants as legitimate hygienic value
rubrics_metrics.description: The impression which plants and plantations make upon our minds and senses is of hygienic value; pleasurable impressions (flowers, tastefully laid-out grounds) contribute to health and well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the hygienic value of plants include psychological benefits (mood, pleasure, appetite stimulation) and their downstream physiological impacts. Consider aesthetic design and public taste as part of health-promoting planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetation's influence on soil and microclimate as hygienic factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetation influences the conformation of the soil and other air qualities (shade in summer, decrease of wind and dust) which are relevant to health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include effects on soil stability, moisture, shade, windbreaks, and dust suppression when evaluating the public-health value of plantations and forests. Reference field studies/meteorological stations focused on forest-culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design requirements for testing plant effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments should measure gas concentrations at various hours of day and night, compare enclosed vegetated spaces (e.g., winter garden) with open air, and control for human presence; repeated measures and careful technique are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow protocols such as repeated sampling across times, accounting for occupancy (people/workers raising CO2), and using appropriate controls (open-air baselines). The winter-garden example shows daytime CO2 can rise due to people more than plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of measurement methodology and instrument precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent variations in gases depend on the methods used; as methods of determining carbonic acid and oxygen were perfected (e.g., Von Bunsen's gas analysis) measured variations became smaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate studies in light of analytical method quality; give more weight to results obtained with improved, reliable measurement techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemiological correlation required to support disease–ozone hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational station data (e.g., Konigsberg ozone-stations) showed diseases came and went without any apparent connection to ozone, arguing against simple causal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal/epidemiological evidence to test putative links between atmospheric constituents (like ozone) and disease incidence rather than relying on speculative or single-point observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hygiene as economic evaluation: quantify 'how much' and 'whether enough'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hygiene must ask not only whether an effect exists but how large it is and whether it is sufficient to matter: 'Hygiene is a science of economics... ask not only what exists and whether it exists, but how much there is and whether enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply cost–benefit reasoning when recommending plantings or expenditures for aesthetic/health ends; require quantitative estimates of effect size before policy or design decisions.
